All praise belongs to God, who brings everything we can sense or understand into being and is the final end of every search and request. May blessings be upon the finest of His servants, the guide who showed creation its beginning and its return—above all, Muhammad, the chosen leader, sent to human beings and jinn. O God, bless him; bless the pure spirits among his family and children, and the radiant figures among his friends and descendants.
The servant in need of his Lord's mercy, the One who is rich beyond all need, Muhammad, known as Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī, says:

Some people think happiness lies in bodily honors or positions of imagined power. But look closely at things and learn to understand them, and you will see that passing pleasures and bodily delights are not true happiness. They bring no joy to the intellect. Those who pursue them become consumed by them. Divine peace leaves them, knowledge of God finds no home in them, and they cannot form a pure intention from the heart of the rational soul. Worldly worries obstruct that intention, while immediate desires press against it. Yet it is pure intention that leads us toward true happiness. It lets us live in pursuit of that happiness and receive the higher outpouring of existence. This lifts the blindness from the soul's eye: the blindness of being confined to this unfamiliar world, dwelling in the house of the body, and losing sight of eternal beauty and everlasting majesty.

The highest goal any being can reach is the particular perfection suited to its nature. Anything below that is, in truth, a deficiency for it, even if it counts as a perfection beside the next lower level of existence. Every animal, and every being beneath it, is naturally disposed to reach the fullest state available to it unless something blocks the way.

Human beings, too, have a perfection unique to their essence and deepest reality. Nothing surpasses us in this, and nothing reaches it before us: it is to know the intelligible realities, draw near to the Creator, and rise beyond matter. At the same time, we share features with beings at lower levels. Like other bodies, we occupy space. Like plants, we take nourishment and grow. Like other animals, we live and breathe, move by choice, and sense. Our distinctive human perfection comes through knowledge and understanding, as the soul loosens its attachment to worldly adornments.

Knowledge has many branches, and the ways of understanding are numerous. It is difficult, perhaps impossible, to master them all. So people have divided their efforts, just as crafts have divided into specialties. Scholars have split into groups and schools: disciplines based on reasoning and those based on received reports, foundations and branches, grammar, syntax, astrology, legal rulings, jurisprudence, the study of religious narrators, and theology.

A thoughtful person should concentrate on what matters most. First, they should learn enough of the other sciences to meet the needs of this life and the next, and free themselves from what obstructs guidance and the Day of Return. Then they should devote their life to the knowledge that can bring their own being to its fullest state.

This knowledge perfects one of the soul's two powers. One belongs to what we are in ourselves and turns toward God; the other concerns our relation to creation and turns toward the created world. The first is our power to understand. It belongs to the soul in its own nature, apart from its connection to the body and the changes the body undergoes. Other fields of knowledge answer needs that come from the body: its powers, its activities, or its desires. Divine wisdom and knowledge of God are different. No other field can, by itself, bring the human soul to completion and free it from its faults when it leaves this world, returns to its deepest reality, and turns wholly toward its Creator, Originator, and Giver.

This pure knowledge of the intellect begins with God: His attributes, His angels, His books, and His messengers. It includes understanding how things flow from Him in the fullest order and how He knows, cares for, and governs them without flaw, weakness, harm, or weariness. It also includes knowledge of the soul: its path to the next life, its union with the highest company, its release from its bonds, and its freedom from matter in its most basic, formless state. Through this knowledge, the soul escapes the narrow limits of possibility and the blows of passing events. It immerses itself in the sea of the spiritual realm, joins the ranks of those who dwell in the world of divine power, and frees itself from captivity to desire, confusion, the effects of motion, and the rule of the turning heavens.
Any other field is useful if it serves this end. If it does not—if it is grammar, language, poetry, or another subject—then it is a craft or skill, like other crafts and skills.

Practical action and worship, both of the heart and of the body, are needed to cleanse and strengthen the soul through religious practice and bodily discipline. Without them, the soul may become attached to the body, its desires, and its demands. It can grow used to obeying the body and serving its appetites. Then, when the body dies, the soul may be kept from the pleasures that belong to it: the company of those brought near to God, the sight of beautiful realities, and the lights of the holy ones.

After death, the body can no longer distract the soul as it once did, keeping it from remembering what lies beyond it. Divine law therefore mercifully commands us to place the powers that rule the body under the rule of the tranquil soul. Religious laws and divine disciplines train the body and its desires, and help the human soul struggle against its own powers. The body can then join the soul in turning toward God, leaving behind the world's false show and source of delusion. It no longer blocks the soul's path; it supports the soul in what it seeks.

From the first years of my youth and early prime, I devoted my strength to divine philosophy as far as my ability and effort allowed. I followed the earlier philosophers and the learned thinkers who came after them. I drew on the results of their thought and insight, learned from the treasures of their minds and their hidden knowledge, and studied what I found in Greek books and the works of the leading teachers. I chose the heart of each subject and avoided needless length.

I avoided chasing distant hopes while doing little, or stretching out arguments as the hour of death drew near, merely to gain an imagined standing or become a leader in name, without gaining anything worthwhile from wisdom or reaching any result through inquiry. Yet many people in our time begin by studying scholars' books with great seriousness and effort. Before long, they grow tired of every subject and settle for only a sip from each jar. They do not find in those books what first drew them to study. Their desires are the desires of the impotent, and their motives those of an embryo. That is why they gain little knowledge, and even the most wretched among them does not become a clear-sighted, happy person.

You see students who hope to spend a long life searching and reviewing, deep into the night and at every turn of the day. In the end, they come back empty-handed, disgraced and ashamed. They are the people described in the Qur'an: “Shall we tell you who will lose most through their deeds? Those whose efforts are wasted in the life of this world, while they think they are doing good.” May God protect us from this bewildering trap and oppressive darkness.

I found shells of knowledge in the vast sea of wisdom. They were braced by dazzling proofs and filled with pearls of rare insight and hidden jewels of fine ideas. For a time, I turned the matter over in my mind, weighed my choices, and spoke inwardly with myself, out of care for those who need the truth.

I wanted to crack open those thick shells and bring out their pearls. I would strain what I found through the filter of thought and sift the kernels from the husks with the sieve of sound judgment. Then I would write a book bringing together the best of earlier thinkers: the clearest arguments of Aristotle's followers, the finest insights of philosophers of illumination and Stoic sages, and new ideas absent from the books of philosophers in every age—ideas unlike anything seen in the turning heavens or the changing world.

But obstacles stood in the way, and the troubles of the times blocked my path. The age kept me from rising to the task, and fate kept me from reaching my goal. I saw ignorance and its lowest forms being raised up, while the fires of ignorance and error were fanned. People were left in a wretched state, and their leaders were weak and foolish.

We have been afflicted with people of dull understanding, whose eyes are blinded to the light and secrets of wisdom. Their insight fails before the light of knowledge, like the eyes of bats in bright sunlight. They call close study of divine matters and careful thought about God's signs an innovation. They regard any departure from the habits of the unthinking crowd as error and deception.

They are like those Hanbalites who read books of transmitted reports without distinguishing what must exist from what may exist, or what has always existed from what came into being. Their thought does not rise above bodies and what belongs to them, or beyond these dark structures and their shadows. Because they hate knowledge and wisdom, they have shut themselves off from sacred divine knowledge and the noble truths that prophets and saints have hinted at, and that philosophers and knowers of God have pointed toward.

So ignorance raises its banner and displays its signs. People turn away from wisdom and its worth, scorn those who know God, and oppose the path of insight. They frighten people away from philosophers and cast out learned, spiritually discerning, and pure people. Yet those who plunge deepest into ignorance and foolishness, and turn furthest from the light of both reason and transmitted knowledge, may rise highest in public favor and respect. As the saying goes: “Many a scholar never entered by knocking at the door of our house, while many an ignorant person walked in without knocking.”

Their leaders have neither virtue nor sound judgment. They wear no cloak of reason or guidance. Their hearts are bare of good manners, and their faces show no sign of goodness. I saw a land where no one valued its secrets or the knowledge of free thinkers. Learning and its secrets had faded; truth and its light had gone out; just ways had been lost; and false opinions had spread. The spring of life had dried up, its trade had failed, and faces once bright had grown dark with disappointment. Seeing all this, I turned away from the people of my time and cut myself off from them. A deadened mind and a rigid nature had made me weary of their hostility and the world's lack of support. I withdrew to a quiet corner, hidden in obscurity and defeat. My hopes were broken. I kept to the duties I owed and worked to repair the harm I had done before God. I was no longer teaching lessons or writing books.

To study the sciences and crafts, contribute to discussions, solve difficult problems, explain their aims, or clear up what is obscure, we need a clear mind. We need an imagination free from weariness and confusion, orderly circumstances, and peace of mind.

How can anyone find such calm amid the troubles they hear and see among the people of this age? People write of a lack of fairness and a rise in injustice, of the best and most capable being brought low while the lowest and worst are raised up, and of ignorant, harmful people pretending to be accomplished scholars and expert teachers. These are only some of the many wrongs and public harms that fill our times. In such conditions, even speaking with people and answering their questions becomes difficult—let alone solving the hardest problems and making obscure matters clear.
As one of my brothers put it in Persian:
Do not pour pearls of speech into every ear; let each ear keep its treasure sealed. Not every question calls for words in reply. A seeing eye will excuse lips that stay closed.

At first, I followed the example of my master, guide, and support: the first of the Imams and trustees, the father of the martyred Imams, the ally of the saints, the one who apportions Paradise and Fire. He practised caution and lived among the wicked, cut off from the position of leadership and with few supporters. He turned away from this world and chose the next. The Messenger of God called him his master, his brother, his cousin, and his companion through every great and small affair.

I weighed the two choices he described: should I strike out with a powerless hand, or endure a blind darkness in which the old grow older, the young turn grey, and a believer toils until meeting their Lord? So I followed his example a second time. I judged that patience was wiser. I endured, with a speck in my eye and a lump in my throat. I stopped involving myself with people or keeping their company. I gave up on finding friendship and comfort among them. It became easy to bear the world's hostility and the opposition of those of my time. Their approval and disapproval no longer mattered to me; I became indifferent to their praise and their harm.

I turned wholeheartedly toward the One who brings about every cause and prayed with all my strength to the One who makes hard things easy. I remained hidden, withdrawn, and unknown for a long time. The long discipline kindled a light within me, and the many spiritual exercises set my heart ablaze. Lights from the unseen realm poured over me; hidden truths from the world of divine power came to rest within me. The light of God's oneness reached me, and His kindness came to my aid.

I came to know secrets that had never before opened to me. Meanings that had not been clear through proof now became clear through direct vision. Everything I had previously learned by argument became something I could see for myself, together with further glimpses of divine secrets, heavenly truths, and hidden realities. Morning and evening, the intellect drew breath from the light of truth. It drew near, became intimate with it, and found rest and relief.

With my outward hands I dug into the earth, and water poured out in a stream. With the inner work of thought, I gathered what I had found for those seeking it, and it became a surging sea. Valleys of understanding flowed from this outpouring according to their capacity. Streams of reason ran from it as well. The valleys brought bright jewels and precious pearls to the shores of hearing; the streams grew fresh blossoms and fruit along their banks.

Divine mercy and care do not neglect anything people need according to their capacity. They do not withhold what can benefit their lives. So God's mercy required that the truths revealed to me should not remain hidden. The lights that flow from the Light of lights should not stay concealed. God inspired me to share a drink of what we had tasted with those who thirst for it, and to offer a glimpse of what we had found to hearts clouded by darkness. Whoever drinks from it may come alive; whoever sees it may have their heart lit up.

The appointed time for the book had come. God willed it to appear when He had chosen, through the person He had prepared. I resolved to bring it from possibility into actuality, from concealment into view. I turned my mind to the task and gathered my strength to bring its scattered ideas together. I asked God to strengthen me, lift my burden through His kindness, and open my heart so I could finish it.

My resolve rose after sitting idle; my energy stirred after lying still. My quiet strength woke up, and what had been still began to move. I told myself: “Now is the time to begin. I should set down principles from which further ideas can be drawn, fill people's ears with the finest jewels of meaning, and bring truth into a clear and beautiful form.”

So I wrote this book for those who seek perfection and occupied themselves with it. I set out divine wisdom for those seeking the secrets of the Presence of Beauty and Majesty. The truth almost appears in it as a light made visible, and its hidden meanings are close to being uncovered. God showed me ideas whose lights shine in knowledge of His essence and attributes, although the minds of the wise circle around Him and return exhausted. He inspired me, through the support He gives to whom He wills, with truths whose secrets lead to understanding their source and return, although the minds of the learned circle around them and return disappointed.

Thanks be to God, the writing came out without crookedness or doubt, without hesitation or confusion. It keeps a clear structure: it speaks in symbols when symbols are needed, and gives enough detail when detail is needed. Its ideas are easy to follow, despite their great depth; its subject is lofty, yet its language comes close to the reader.

Divine knowledge is woven into philosophical argument. Truths reached through direct insight are clothed in the language of instruction. Divine secrets are put into familiar words, and difficult ideas are expressed in language close to the ear. The proofs stride forward in brilliant clarity, while the objections of those who miss the truth shrink and are exposed.

Look at the meaning with the eye of your mind. Do you find it lacking? Then look again at the words. Do they seem flawed? I have pointed in its symbols toward treasures of truth that only someone who has worked hard in intellectual discipline can understand. In its chapters I have also drawn attention to principles whose meaning only those who put their bodies through religious discipline will discover, so they can taste the drink for themselves. I wrote it for my brothers in faith and my companions on the path of direct insight and certainty. It will be most useful to those who have studied many earlier thinkers and read the books of the philosophers, without imagining that what they already know is all there is or rejecting everything beyond their present understanding.

Truth cannot be limited to what any one person understands, or measured by any one mind or imagination. If you find something here that goes against what you believe or what seems sound to you, do not reject it. Above everyone with knowledge is someone who knows more. Anyone who is trapped within their own knowledge and rejects everything beyond it has reached the limit of their own learning and remains shut off from the hidden secrets of their Lord.

I do not claim that I have reached the final limit in what I have written. Understanding has more paths than I have found or can count. The truths of God cannot be gathered within the limits I have drawn. If, through divine care, you solve a difficulty or open a difficult question, thank your Lord for the wisdom He has guided you to and praise Him for the gifts He has given you. Follow the teaching of the Lord of the two worlds and mirror of all worlds, may the fullest blessings and purest peace be upon him and his family: “Do not give wisdom to those unworthy of it, or you will lead it astray. Do not withhold it from those worthy of it, or you will wrong it.” Keep wisdom away from dead souls, and entrust it only to living ones.

You should know that I have sometimes gone beyond stating only what I myself hold to be true and believe. I have also presented the approaches of other thinkers, the objections made against them, and the replies to those objections. I have criticized and tested those views, taken them apart, rebuilt their arguments, and defended them as far as I could. I did this to sharpen people's thinking and strengthen their minds. These discussions contain subtle, unfamiliar ways of understanding and elegant ways of reasoning. They train people seeking the truth to solve difficult problems and help students of debate understand questions that are hard to untangle.

The truth is that most of the discussions recorded in books and written on their pages serve mainly to alert us to the ideas of thoughtful people and give us a view of their arguments. They should stir the desire to reach the truth; it is not enough simply to fill the mind with statements, whether rational or transmitted. That alone brings no peace to the heart, no stillness to the soul, no ease to the mind, and no satisfying taste of knowledge. It should instead prepare the seeker to follow the path of the good and reach the hidden truths.

Knowledge of God, knowledge of the Return, and knowledge of the path to the next life do not mean the inherited belief that an ordinary person or a legal scholar may receive second-hand. Someone absorbed in imitation and fixed on outward forms has not opened the path to the truths that open to those close to God. Such a person does not see what is disclosed to those who look beyond the world of appearances and bodily pleasures: knowledge of the Maker of all things and the reality of realities.

Nor is this knowledge simply the skill of argument, as with the theologian, or a chain of abstract debates, as with the philosopher. All of these are layers of darkness, one above another. When a person holds out a hand, they can hardly see it. Whoever God gives no light has no light. True knowledge is a kind of certainty born from a light God casts into the believer's heart, through closeness to the world of holiness and purity, and through struggle against ignorance, bad character, love of power, attachment to the earth, and fascination with the body's ornaments.

I often ask God to forgive me for wasting part of my life following the views and fine distinctions of philosophers and theologians who relied on debate, learning their clever tricks of speech and their skill in debate. In the end, by the light of faith and God's generous support, I saw that their reasoning was fruitless and their path crooked. So we handed the reins of our affairs to God and to His Messenger, the one who warns and gives warning. Whatever came to us from him, we believed and affirmed. We did not force an imagined rational interpretation or argumentative theory upon it. We followed his guidance and stopped where he told us to stop, in keeping with God's words: “Take what the Messenger gives you, and refrain from what he forbids you.” Then God opened my heart to what He opened it to, and, by following the Messenger, I succeeded.

My dear friend, before you read this book, begin by purifying yourself of your desires. Those who cleanse the soul succeed; those who bury it fail. First build a firm foundation of knowledge and wisdom, then climb to its heights. Otherwise, you will be like someone whose building collapses from its foundations, bringing the roof down with it.

Do not busy yourself with the empty talk of ignorant people who call themselves Sufis, and do not accept every claim made by philosophers. Both are misleading trials that can pull you from the right path. They are like those who, when their messengers brought them clear signs, were pleased with the knowledge they already had; then the very things they mocked surrounded them. May God protect both you and me from the harm of these two groups, and keep us apart from them, even for a moment.
Know that the realized mystics and saints undertake four journeys. The first is from creation to God.
The second is through God, in God. The third mirrors the first: it is from God back to creation, through God. The fourth mirrors the second in one respect: it is through God in creation.

I arranged this book to follow their movement through the lights and effects, dividing it into four journeys, and named it Transcendent Wisdom in the Four Intellectual Journeys. I now turn to the subject, seeking help from God, the One worshipped, the Self-Sufficient and Self-Subsisting.

These are the four journeys. The first and third oppose one another because their starting and ending points are reversed. The third journey is carried out through God, unlike the first. The second and fourth are opposites in one respect: they begin and end at different points, but both take place through God.

The great philosophers and firmly grounded sages look at the horizons and within themselves. There they see God's signs shining forth. The effects of His power show them that His existence is necessary; the light of His wisdom reveals the holiness of His names and attributes. The heavens and earth exist, yet they could have been otherwise, and they move. These facts point to God. Their precise construction and ordered arrangement show His knowledge and care for creation.

The Qur'an says: “We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves, until it becomes clear to them that He is the Truth.” At this point, they see that every being and every perfection is absorbed in God's existence and perfection. Every being and every perfection is a glimmer of His light and a display of His presence. This is the first of the four intellectual journeys, corresponding to the spiritual traveler's journey from creation to God.

Next, they study existence itself. They recognize that it must exist through itself, and use this necessity to show that God is simple and one, and that He knows, has power, lives, wills, hears, sees, speaks, and possesses every other quality of perfection and beauty. They see that all these qualities are identical with His essence. His oneness reveals that He is absolutely one. Because He is one in this way, He depends on nothing; and in that complete self-sufficiency, He contains all things in the fullest and highest way. This is the second intellectual journey, corresponding to the spiritual traveler's journey from God to God, through God.

Then they study God's existence, care, and oneness. They discover that He acts as one, and consider how the many things come from Him and are ordered in sequence: the chain of intellects and souls, the higher and lower worlds of divine power and spirit, and, finally, the material world. “Is your Lord not witness over all things?” This is the third intellectual journey, corresponding to the spiritual traveler's journey from God to creation, through God.

Finally, they study how the heavens and earth were created and learn that everything returns to God. They examine the benefits and harms of created things and what brings happiness or misery in this life and the next. They learn how people live and what awaits them after death. With that knowledge, they warn against corruption and call people toward what is good. They study the next life and learn about Paradise and Fire, reward and punishment, the path, the reckoning, the balance, the scattering of records, and the way actions take visible form—in short, everything the prophets brought and the messengers reported, peace and blessings be upon them all. This is the fourth intellectual journey, corresponding to the spiritual traveler's journey from creation to creation, through God.

The book's discussion of general principles, substances, and qualities covers the first journey. Its proof of God's existence through Himself, and its account of His attributes, cover the second. Its proof of holy substances and souls that exist apart from matter covers the third. Its account of the soul and what awaits it on the Day of Resurrection covers the fourth.

So when the author says, “Know that the mystics and saints have four journeys,” he is referring to the spiritual journeys described first. When he says, “I arranged my book,” he is referring to the four intellectual journeys covered by the book and arranged to match the journeys of the spiritual travelers and saints. The powers of understanding and action mirror each other. Through understanding, a person reaches certainty by learning; through action, they reach the certainty of direct sight and the fuller certainty of lived experience. This is what I have understood by considering the words of these thinkers and following the discussions in the book. God knows best.
This account of the four journeys and their relation to the subjects of the book is by the divine philosopher Muḥammad Riḍā al-Iṣfahānī al-Qumshaʾī. May his memory be blessed.

As long as a person has not begun the intellectual journey of study and reflection, they see multiplicity everywhere and overlook unity. They see every thing as one among many, and that multiplicity keeps them from seeing unity. Unity remains hidden behind the many things they see.

When they begin their intellectual journey from effects to their cause, and from created things to their Maker, the many things slowly fade from view into the single, absolute, true unity. At last, they see no multiplicity at all. They become so absorbed in unity that they no longer look at individual things. At this stage, unity hides multiplicity, and the traveler sees nothing but unity. This is the stage of inward experience that corresponds to the first journey: from creation to God, or from multiplicity to unity.

Once the traveler reaches the world of unity and no longer sees multiplicity, they use intellectual reflection to move from God's essence and oneness to His attributes, names, and acts, one by one. They come to know the qualities of His necessary existence in a clear and ordered way. This is the second journey. It takes place in God because it concerns His attributes, names, and qualities. It takes place through God because the traveler is now grounded in God's reality and has turned away from the separate existence of the self and all other things. The traveler remains through God’s own abiding, not merely because God keeps the traveler in existence. Understand this, if you know these secrets.

At this stage, the traveler's heart may open. Their words may no longer be bound by feelings of helplessness. They may see multiplicity within unity and unity within multiplicity: seeing unity does not block their view of the many, and seeing the many does not distract them from unity. They can hold both worlds together. This comes from the breadth of their being and the openness of their heart. They can then teach those who are not yet complete and guide people whose minds and souls are still weak.

This stage of spiritual and intellectual travel corresponds to the journey from God back to creation, through God. It is the stage of prophecy and messengership. Above it is another stage, higher, more complete, more subtle, and more exact: proving the existence of God and of everything else through God, without placing anything between God and the proof. This is called the proof of the truthful. A person does not need to reach this stage in order to teach, guide, or be a prophet or messenger. It is a perfection of the person in relation to themselves. It is linked to the second journey, because becoming grounded in God's reality entails it, but teaching and guidance depend only on the first and second journeys. This highest stage corresponds to the fourth journey: through God in creation.

The correspondence between the four journeys described in the book and these four spiritual stages is as follows. The book's discussions of general principles, substances, qualities, and the states of existing things and their essences form the first journey: from creation to God. Its discussion of God—proving His existence, and considering His attributes, names, and actions—is the second journey, which takes place in God through God.

This second journey also contains the fourth journey, through God in creation. Anyone who follows the book's discussion of divine matters will see that it includes proof of the One who must exist, then uses His existence to show that everything else depends on Him.

The third journey is the journey of the soul. It studies the soul from the beginning of its development to its return to God, from its first weakness to its fullest perfection and strength. This is the third journey: from God to creation, through God. Keep all this in mind.

This account is by the learned Mīrzā Muḥammad Ḥasan al-Nūrī, son of the divine philosopher Mullā ʿAlī al-Nūrī. May God keep their secrets holy. The careful investigator Kamāl al-Dīn ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Kāshānī says:

A journey is the heart's turning toward God. There are four journeys. The first is the journey to God: moving through the stages of the self until reaching the clear horizon, the end of the heart's development and the beginning of the display of God's names.
The second is the journey in God: taking on His qualities and realizing His names until reaching the highest horizon and the end of the realm of divine oneness.
